lines.text: They don't see you.
They hear you.
And the store radio just told every one of them... where you are.

lines.text: An hour ago, the customers stopped being customers.

lines.text: Nine thousand cans.
Thirty-eight gallons of water.
Two batteries.
Food is not the problem.
Rule one. They hear. They don't see.

lines.text: At two thirty-one, somewhere in aisle twelve, an alarm clock starts to ring.

lines.text: Nobody here set that alarm.
This is your first week inside Freshway.
You'll make four rules. You'll learn how they hunt.
And you'll find out you're not alone in this store.
You'll survive it. Not because you're lucky.
Because of one decision you make on day six.
Back to two thirty-one. The ringing comes from aisle twelve.
And every dead thing in this store turns toward it.
There are four of them in here with you.
Darlene from the register. Mike, the night guard. A lady who came in for milk at midnight.
And Gary.
Three of them shuffle toward aisle twelve.
Gary doesn't. Gary walks to his office. Like he does every night at two thirty.
He closes the door behind him. Habit.
Problem one. Three dead people. One store. And you.
Here's what you know. They follow sound. They don't see.
And the stockroom has a walk-in freezer.
Steel door. Four inches of foam in the walls.
Sound goes in. Nothing comes out.
You don't have a weapon. You have a phone.
Thirty-one percent battery. No signal. But it still has an alarm.
You set it for two fifty.
You put it on the freezer floor and prop the door open with a box of frozen peas.
Then you climb.
These shelves are eight feet tall and rated for a thousand pounds. You're fine.
At two forty-eight, the clock in aisle twelve gives up.
And the store goes very quiet.
Three of them. One freezer. Minus eighteen degrees.
Problem one, solved.
You also just locked your only phone in a freezer with three dead people.
So. Mostly solved.
One more thing. Every walk-in freezer has a safety release on the inside. So nobody gets trapped.
You really hope they never figure out how it works.
Six forty-one in the morning. You haven't slept.
And then you remember what happens at seven.
Freshway opens at seven. Every day. Automatically.
The lights come on. The music starts. And the front doors unlock.
There are two hundred of them outside those doors.
Most of them are regulars.
Problem two. The store opens in nineteen minutes.
The schedule runs from one room. The manager's office. Gary's office.
Gary is standing at his desk. Facing the clock. Waiting for his shift to end.
The control panel is on the wall behind him.
To reach it, you have to pass within arm's reach of a dead man who can hear a sneeze through a wall.
Shoes off. Socks only. Heel, then toe.
Six fifty-eight.
His keys hang from his belt. Fourteen of them. If they jingle, you're done.
The switch says open. You push it to closed.
The doors stay locked. You did it.
What you don't know is that the music runs on its own timer.
Good morning, Freshway shoppers! We're open!
Two hundred dead people hear the Freshway jingle. At the same time.
You find the speaker cable in four seconds. It feels like forty.
The doors hold.
Rule two. Music is a dinner bell.
On your way out, you take Gary's keys off his belt. Very slowly.
And you lock him in his own office.
In three years, it's the first time you've seen him stay past noon.
Day one. You do something Gary never did. You read the building manual.
Freshway is thirty thousand square feet. Fourteen rows of shelves.
One front entrance. One loading dock. One fire exit. And a ladder to the roof.
The front has steel shutters. The dock has a roll-up door. The fire exit has a magnetic lock.
That's the one that worries you.
Magnetic locks are fail-safe. If the power goes out, they open. So nobody gets trapped in a fire.
Great for fires. Terrible for this.
At the security desk, you find a charging dock for the store radios.
Two slots. One radio.
You figure the night guard took the other one home.
Here's the thing about the power. It's still on.
Somewhere, a power plant is running with nobody in it.
Without people to balance it, a power grid doesn't last long. Days, maybe.
When it goes, three things happen.
The exit signs switch to batteries. Ninety minutes of light. That's the building code.
The freezer starts warming. A closed freezer stays frozen for about two days.
And the fire exit unlocks.
Problem three. The back door.
So you build a wall.
Forty bags of dog food. Six pallets of bottled water. A display of discounted patio chairs.
It takes eleven hours. It's the best thing you've ever built.
Water is no longer the problem. Most of it is holding a door shut.
Day two. Sunset. You climb to the roof for the first time.
And you count them.
Two hundred and twelve. Standing in the parking lot. Facing the front doors.
They don't sit. They don't sleep. They wait for the store to open.
Across the street is Brookfield Mall. Four floors. Every window dark.
Except one. Top floor. A light.
Someone over there is alive.
Day three. Eleven forty at night.
The radio on your belt clicks.
Freshway. Anyone in Freshway. Come back.
A man's voice. Calm. Tired.
This is Dale. Mall security, across the street. I saw your flashlight on the roof.
You haven't heard a living voice in three days.
I'm here.
Good. Keep it quiet. They come to voices.
How many of you are there?
Just me.
Just you. Okay.
Dale talks for an hour. He knows things.
He knows they don't see. He knows the front lot is full.
And that alarm at two thirty-one. You heard that too, right?
You never mentioned the alarm.
You figure the sound carries across the street.
Day four. Three fifteen in the afternoon.
The fridges stop humming.
The lights go out. All of them. At once.
The exit signs blink to battery. Ninety minutes.
And at the back of the store...
...the fire exit unlocks.
Fourteen of them are on the loading dock. They heard it.
Your wall moves an inch. Then another.
Dog food was a mistake.
You need them away from that door. And you need something louder than a door.
One shopping cart. Forty cans of soup. A twenty-foot drop.
You push it off the far side of the roof.
Every dead thing in the lot turns toward the noise. Even the ones at your door.
It's the most fun you've had all week.
What would you have thrown? Tell me in the comments.
Day five. You have a routine now.
You sleep in a two-person tent in aisle nine. Camping and outdoors.
Cold peaches for breakfast. Every day.
At seven sharp, Gary bangs on his office door.
Gary has never been late a day in his life. Or after it.
And at night, you talk to Dale.
Rate your day, Freshway. One to ten.
Four.
Four's good. Four's alive.
He tells bad jokes. He asks about you. He asks what you've got.
How much water? How much food?
You tell him.
And the freezer? Still holding?
You stop.
You never told Dale about the freezer.
Maybe you did. It's been a long week.
That night, at two thirty-one...
...the alarm in aisle twelve starts to ring.
You took the batteries out of that clock on the first night.
They're still in your pocket.
Someone put new ones in.
Day six. Dale has an idea.
Come over to the mall. We've got a generator. Hot food. Twelve people.
Twelve people. Hot food. A door that locks.
But you can't cross that lot with two hundred of them in it.
So you make a plan. Rule one is still the rule. They follow sound.
Aisle eleven has alarm clocks. Six of them. Four ninety-nine each.
You set them one minute apart. Two-oh-one to two-oh-six.
You'll throw them from the roof to the far end of the lot. One by one, they'll pull the crowd away.
Eighty meters to the mall's side door. Ninety seconds if you walk.
You won't run. Running is loud.
And don't bring anything. We've got plenty. Just come.
So you pack light. Water. A flashlight. And Gary's keys.
You don't know why. You just never told Dale about the keys.
Day seven. Two in the morning. You're on the roof.
You throw the clocks. Six of them. Into the dark.
Two-oh-one. The crowd turns. Slowly. Like grass in the wind.
Two-oh-two. Two-oh-three. The front lot empties toward the far corner.
You climb down the back ladder.
Stop. Don't move.
Okay. Keep coming.
Halfway across, Dale talks again.
Don't stop now, kid.
And you hear it twice.
Once in your radio. And once, faint, from behind you.
From the roof of Freshway.
Dale was never at the mall.
That light in the window? Nobody's turned it off in six days. Because nobody's there.
He's been in your store the whole week.
He knew about the alarm. He knew about the freezer.
He never wanted you at the mall. He wanted you out of Freshway.
With nothing.
Every can. Every gallon. His now.
And the alarms are dying. One by one.
Two-oh-six. The last clock stops.
Two hundred of them start walking back.
Now you run.
Not to the roof. Not to the dock. To the staff door on the side of the building.
Steel door. Key lock. And you have Gary's keys.
Fourteen keys. No labels.
Gary labeled every shelf in that store. Not one key.
The fourth one turns.
You're inside. You lock it behind you.
You survive this week. Not because you were lucky. Because you kept one thing to yourself.
Day seven. Here's what you know.
Rule one. They hear. They don't see.
Rule two. Music is a dinner bell.
Rule three. Count the radios.
Rule four. Never tell anyone what you have.
Two thirty-one.
The radio clicks.
You came back.
This is my store.
In aisle twelve, the alarm starts to ring.
That... That's not me.

pa.text: Attention, Freshway shoppers. Aisle seven is now open.
